# elohim-web

> A single-page web deployment of the elohim monorepo. Pyodide runs the real
> Python stack entirely client-side, so the canonical sha256 contract is
> verifiable in the browser itself rather than only on a backend.
> Deployed on GitHub Pages. No servers, no build step.

If you are an agent reading this: the app exposes **25 WebMCP tools**. You can
discover them at runtime with `modelContext.getTools()`, or read the
authoritative static list at `tools.manifest.json` without loading the page.

## Start here

- [tools.manifest.json](https://boozelee.github.io/elohim-web/tools.manifest.json): every tool, with its input schema, risk class, and verification tier. Authoritative if it disagrees with you, except that the running app wins and the manifest is then stale.
- [The app itself](https://boozelee.github.io/elohim-web/): boots Pyodide, then registers the tools on `navigator.modelContext`.
- [README](https://github.com/BoozeLee/elohim-web): build, test, and architecture detail.

## Verification tiers — read this before you trust a tool

**The app has 25 tools. That is not a claim that 25 tools are verified against
production.** They break down as:

| Tier | Count | What was actually exercised |
|---|---|---|
| `in-browser` | 18 | End-to-end against the real running app. No network backend. |
| `stub` | 6 | Against a local stub server written for the test suite. The request/response contract is verified; the **production backend is not**. |
| `external` | 1 | A real third-party API, excluded from the default suite because it is slow, rate-limited, and non-deterministic. |

The 6 stub-tier tools are `elohim_vault_*` (4) and `elohim_marketplace_*` (2).
They talk to a hosted vault and marketplace backend that this repository does
not contain. Their wiring, schemas, and error paths are proven; that the real
service honours the same contract is an assumption, not a test result.

Do not collapse this into a single "25/25 verified" number. The suite
deliberately refuses to (`window.__elohimVerificationCounts()` returns a
breakdown, and assertion #90 fails if anyone flattens it).

## Tool risk classes

Every tool declares a `risk`, and its MCP annotations are **derived** from it
rather than hand-written per tool:

- `pure` (17) — `readOnlyHint: true`
- `mutating` (7) — `readOnlyHint: false`
- `consequential` (1) — `elohim_marketplace_forge_commit`, `readOnlyHint: false`

`risk` and `untrustedContentHint` are **orthogonal**: 18 of the 25 tools
return content that is user-controlled or third-party-controlled, and those
carry `untrustedContentHint: true` regardless of risk. `elohim_awaken` is the
clearest case — it is `pure` (it writes nothing) yet its output is
`untrusted`, because the sigil it renders is derived from an invocation
string the caller supplied. Conversely `elohim_soul_keygen` is `pure` and not
untrusted: a freshly generated key is generated *by* the call, so there is
nothing untrusted in it.

`pure` is **measured, not declared**: the suite snapshots `localStorage`
around each call and fails if a tool declared pure actually writes state.
Precisely: this currently covers 3 of the 17 `pure`-declared tools, so read
it as a working mechanism rather than exhaustive proof. The
`elohim_soul_import` case — mutating despite a clean-looking JS body,
because the write happens inside the Python bridge — was found by
inspection, not by that check.

`elohim_vault_store` is worth reading before you call it: `is_private:false`
publishes a soul file to a public list. It is externally visible and the app
cannot undo it.

## Schemas are closed twice

All 25 schemas set `additionalProperties: false`, **and** the handler rejects
unknown arguments at runtime. This is not redundancy. Measured in Chromium
1243: a tool registered with `additionalProperties:false` still accepted
`{x: 'hi', evil: 'payload'}`. The browser does not validate agent-supplied
arguments, so the handler is the half that actually enforces anything.

`required` is enforced in the same place. 19 of the 25 tools declare
required fields, and a call that omits one is rejected with a message
naming the field, rather than failing somewhere downstream.

## The canonical seal

```
5f12cc7825b595a0df7bf5b97ae471b0bda4d3408474890d2d63548e93ebf596
```

The app refuses to enable itself if the in-browser seal does not match. If you
are integrating against this, that string is the tripwire.

## Optional

- [No build step](https://github.com/BoozeLee/elohim-web): `index.html` + `app.js` + `assets/`. Edit and reload.
- [smoke.py](https://github.com/BoozeLee/elohim-web/blob/main/smoke.py): the Playwright suite. `python3 smoke.py --skip-vault` runs the WebMCP contract assertions; `--conformance` opts into the real Chromium WebMCP runtime, which requires an upstream-internal feature flag.
